performers: Soojin Han, violin; Hankyung Arte Philharmonic; Seokwon Hong, conductor
intro: After one bar of orchestra, Soojin Han begins the long melody of Mendelssohn’s E minor concerto. Later, the cadenza turns inside out: her arpeggios become the accompaniment while the orchestra takes back the tune.

sections.mNote: One bar of strings before the solo melody

sections.label: A′ · The orchestra takes the tune
sections.mNote: The soloist rests during the orchestra’s fortissimo reply

sections.label: Dev · The violin reworks its opening

sections.mNote: Chords, trills and arpeggios before the theme returns

cues.title: One bar, then the violin
cues.text: One bar of murmuring strings, then the solo violin begins its E-minor melody. Clarinets and bassoons hold their notes; the basses pluck underneath. Mendelssohn gives the soloist the first word, quietly, before the orchestra has had a tune of its own.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, plate M.B. 18, p. 1, bars 1–8. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP24558-PMLP04931-Mendelssohn_Violin_Concerto_Op.64.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A tune without peace
cues.text: On 30 July 1838, Mendelssohn writes to Ferdinand David, leader of Leipzig’s Gewandhaus Orchestra: “I’d like to write a violin concerto for you next winter; one in E minor sticks in my head, the beginning of which will not leave me in peace.”
cues.evidence: Mendelssohn to Ferdinand David, 30 July 1838, quoted by Steven Ledbetter in the Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note. https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto

cues.title: The soloist plays the bass
cues.text: The violin descends to its open G string and stays there. Flutes and clarinets sing the new G-major tune above it, marked tranquillo. For this first phrase the soloist supplies the bass; the orchestral strings are silent.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 9. Steven Ledbetter describes the high C, descent to open G and wind melody: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The opening starts to wander
cues.text: After a held chord, the violin picks up its opening melody again over quiet strings and plucked basses. Soon it is running through scales while the woodwinds answer. The two tunes of the exposition now meet inside the development.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 10–11. The combination of the two themes is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: David plays; Gade conducts
cues.text: Leipzig, 13 March 1845: Ferdinand David gives the concerto’s first performance with the Gewandhaus Orchestra. Mendelssohn is ill, so Niels Gade conducts. The promise of a concerto “next winter” has taken nearly seven years to reach the platform.
cues.evidence: Première date, performers and Mendelssohn’s illness: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Mendelssohn). Steven Ledbetter also records the première and quotes the promise in the letter of 30 July 1838: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto

cues.title: The cadenza takes over
cues.text: In the cadenza, the violin has the stage to itself: chords, wide leaps, trills and arpeggios. Mendelssohn places this solo passage in the middle of the movement, before the opening tune returns. Its last arpeggios will keep going when the orchestra comes back.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 17–18, Cadenza ad libitum and recapitulation. The cadenza’s structural position is discussed by Steven Ledbetter: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The solo becomes an accompaniment
cues.text: The opening melody returns in flutes, oboes and first violins. Beneath it, the soloist’s arpeggios keep rippling across the strings, pianissimo. The cadenza has carried straight into the recapitulation; the violin that began alone now accompanies its own tune.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 18: returning theme above the soloist’s continuing semiquaver arpeggios.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The wind tune comes home
cues.text: The second tune returns in E major. The violin holds a low E while the woodwinds sing; oboes and bassoons now join the flutes and clarinets. G♯ warms the home key before the movement turns back to E minor.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 20: E-major second subject, sustained solo E and four woodwind pairs.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Faster, then faster again
cues.text: The closing stretch returns to E minor and gathers speed. Mendelssohn writes Più presto, then Sempre più presto, and finally Presto. The violin’s runs cut through wind chords and the strings’ insistent off-beat accents.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 24–27; the successive tempo markings appear on pp. 25–26.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One bassoon refuses to stop
cues.text: The first movement closes in E minor, but the first bassoon holds on to B after the other instruments finish. That single note carries into the Andante. It will rise a semitone to C as the slow movement begins.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 27, the join to the Andante. The sustained bassoon and connected movements are also described by Steven Ledbetter: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The violin’s ascent summons the orchestra
transitions.from: A · The violin begins in E minor
transitions.to: A′ · The orchestra takes the tune
transitions.how: The violin’s rising scales lead to full orchestral chords in E minor. Flutes, oboes and first violins take up the opening melody at fortissimo; lower strings strike repeated chords beneath them. The solo violin rests while its tune fills the orchestra.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 4: rising solo scales and orchestral statement of the first theme.

transitions.title: The violin descends beneath the woodwinds
transitions.to: B · Woodwinds sing over the violin’s G
transitions.how: From a high C, the solo violin descends to its lowest note, open G. The orchestral strings stop, leaving that G as the bass of the new G-major tune. Flutes and clarinets sing above it, pianissimo and tranquillo.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 9. Steven Ledbetter describes the descent and inverted soloist–orchestra roles: https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto

transitions.title: A held chord, then plucked basses
transitions.from: B · Woodwinds sing over the violin’s G
transitions.to: Dev · The violin reworks its opening
transitions.how: A pianissimo G-major chord with a fermata ends the exposition. The soloist resumes the opening melody over quiet strings; plucked bass notes mark the pulse. As the violin rises, the accompaniment grows and the wind instruments begin to answer.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 10–11: fermata at the end of the exposition and the soft beginning of the development.

transitions.title: A held B opens the cadenza
transitions.from: Dev · The violin reworks its opening
transitions.how: Over B in the bass, the orchestra grows from pianissimo to fortissimo, marked poco a poco crescendo. The dominant of E minor remains unresolved as the orchestra drops out. The violin continues alone under the heading Cadenza ad libitum, with the return of the opening theme still ahead.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 17: crescendo over B and the beginning of the cadenza.

transitions.title: Arpeggios carry across the join
transitions.to: A″ · The orchestra sings over arpeggios
transitions.how: The cadenza settles into continuous semiquaver arpeggios. Flutes, oboes and first violins enter with the E-minor opening melody while the soloist keeps playing, now pianissimo. Low strings restore the accompaniment beneath both. There is no pause between solo display and the return.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 17–18, end of the cadenza and opening of the recapitulation.

transitions.title: The violin rests on low E
transitions.from: A″ · The orchestra sings over arpeggios
transitions.to: B′ · The wind tune in E major
transitions.how: The violin descends as the orchestra diminishes, sempre più tranquillo. Its sustained low E becomes the bass under the woodwinds’ second theme. The tune first heard in G major now comes in E major, with oboes and bassoons added to the flutes and clarinets.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 20: descending solo line, sustained E and the wind theme in E major.

transitions.title: E minor begins the final chase
transitions.from: B′ · The wind tune in E major
transitions.to: Coda · E minor, faster and faster
transitions.how: E minor returns for the closing stretch. The solo violin runs above off-beat string chords while the winds recall the opening tune. Mendelssohn then tightens the pace through Più presto, Sempre più presto and Presto, sending the violin into another chain of scales.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 24–26: closing E-minor passage and successive faster tempo markings.

source.title: Mendelssohn, Violin Concerto in E minor, Op. 64, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel; Rietz edition, Serie 4 No. 18)
source.locator: I. Allegro molto appassionato, pp. 1–27: opening solo, p. 1; orchestral reply, p. 4; wind theme, p. 9; cadenza and return, pp. 17–18; E-major theme, p. 20; close, pp. 24–27.

timeline.note: The violin begins in the second bar, above murmuring strings, held clarinet and bassoon notes, and plucked basses.
The orchestra takes the opening tune at fortissimo while the solo violin rests.
Flutes and clarinets sing above the soloist’s open G string; the orchestral strings are silent.
The solo violin takes the G-major tune, and the strings return softly beneath it.
The violin begins the development over quiet strings, with the basses plucking the pulse.
The soloist’s running notes continue against the full orchestra’s chords.
The violin’s arpeggios and murmuring strings grow quieter beneath sustained woodwind notes.
The orchestra rests throughout the solo violin’s cadenza.
Flutes, oboes and first violins bring back the opening tune over the soloist’s pianissimo arpeggios.
The orchestra’s fortissimo reply fills out the returning E-minor theme.
Flutes, oboes and clarinets sing the E-major theme above the violin’s held E; bassoons and horns join later in the phrase.
The violin’s running notes and the orchestra’s accented chords gather speed towards the close.

fields.note: The video description on the YouTube channel named “한수진 Soojin Han” reads “Vn. Soojin Han / Cond. Seokwon Hong / Orch. Hankyung Arte Philharmonic”. The Commons file page names only the orchestra as author, linking the orchestra’s own site. That site’s news column reports a later concert (September 2026) played by the orchestra under a conductor named 홍석원 (Hong Seok-won, professor at Seoul National University), which supports the association but says nothing about the 2022 concert. No roster of players is given, and no second source for the soloist was opened.

composer.epithet: At sixteen, he made eight string players sound like the most exhilarating orchestra in Europe.
facts: Ludwig Berger, piano; Carl Friedrich Zelter, composition
Düsseldorf music director, 1833–35; Leipzig Gewandhaus conductor from 1835
Married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children; brother of Fanny Hensel
Leipzig Conservatoire, founded 1843; ten visits to Britain
composer.background:
In 1825, sixteen-year-old Felix Mendelssohn wrote a birthday present for his violin teacher, Eduard Rietz. It required four violins, two violas and two cellos, and gave Rietz a first-violin part that climbs out over the other seven players in long, buoyant arcs. The E♭ major Octet still sounds like someone discovering how much pleasure eight string instruments can make. Eleven years later, its composer played second viola in a public performance. Writing to Karl Klingemann on 31 January 1836, he admitted to “heart palpitations”.

He had been noisy from the start. In 1812, his sister Fanny wrote to friends in Hamburg: “Felix has a strong voice and sings all day.” He was born there on 3 February 1809; the family moved to Berlin two years later. His father Abraham was a banker, his grandfather Moses the Jewish philosopher. Abraham and Lea Mendelssohn had their children baptised as Christians in 1816 and used the additional surname Bartholdy. Fanny and Felix learnt piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter.
